strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial inference cost of diffusion-based language models.
SlowFast Sampling provides an intuitive two-stage mechanism that dynamically switches between cautious exploration and aggressive parallel decoding using confidence, stability, and position.

The evaluation covers two representative dLLMs and eight reasoning, knowledge, and coding benchmarks. The reported 2.1–5.24× standalone throughput improvements generally come with modest quality changes.
The method appears compatible with an existing caching approach, and the sensitivity experiments examine all principal thresholds used by the proposed heuristic.
weaknesses: The method is not specified precisely enough to reproduce. Values for k_slow and k_fast are missing, the duration and termination rule of the fast phase are unclear, and generation length, diffusion-step count, block configuration, batch size, precision, timing protocol, and software environment are largely unspecified. The manuscript also provides no usable code link.

There are consequential ambiguities and contradictions in the algorithm. Equation 9 defines the cycle endpoint as the mean of recent candidates, while the following sentence sets it to the last candidate. Rounding, empty candidate sets, span boundaries, and the update s_cycle <- e_cycle are not handled. It is also unclear how caching predicted values outside a span avoids Transformer computation, since positions are ordinarily processed jointly.

The three claimed 'golden principles' receive little empirical validation. Figure 1 is essentially a single illustrative trajectory rather than a quantitative analysis across examples, layers, models, or tasks. Certainty-based unmasking is already standard, and the paper does not adequately establish the novelty or generality of the convergence and positional observations.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. The main tables mostly compare against each model's default sampler; Table 3 compares only a few broadly defined strategies on one benchmark. Most importantly, there is no dLLM-Cache-only baseline, so the claimed compatibility benefit and the contribution of SlowFast Sampling to the combined 34.22× result cannot be isolated.

Several reported results are inconsistent or insufficiently contextualized. For GPQA, LLaDA has 3.31 TPS in Table 1 but 1.60 TPS in Table 4; for GSM8K, SlowFast obtains 14.57 TPS in Table 1 but 9.87 TPS in Table 3 despite the same reported score. No explanation or controlled configuration is given.

The headline comparison with LLaMA3 is not fully convincing: SlowFast alone remains slower (25.00 versus 33.79 TPS), while exceeding LLaMA3 requires caching and reduces GPQA accuracy from 31.92 to as low as 28.79. The comparison also lacks evidence that decoding lengths, hardware utilization, implementations, precision, and batching are matched fairly.

Ablations are confined to GSM8K, provide no repeated-run variability or statistical uncertainty, and do not ablate the three principles or the slow and fast stages individually. Consequently, the paper does not show which proposed components actually cause the gains.

The presentation contains numerous grammatical and typographical issues, crowded tables, and overstrong claims such as 'lossless acceleration' and surpassing autoregressive models in practicality. Overall, the promising empirical signal is outweighed by underspecification, weak baseline controls, and insufficient support for the central claims.

The duration and termination of the fast stage, handling of the global diffusion schedule, values of k_slow and k_fast, rounding of the mean endpoint, and cache invalidation are omitted. Low variance of this scalar endpoint, especially with W_hist=2, does not establish that the entire span is safe for aggressive decoding.

There is no cache-only baseline in Table 2, no component ablation isolating the proposed principles or slow/fast stages, and only a very limited comparison with other acceleration or adaptive-sampling methods. Hyperparameter studies on one model and one benchmark do not fill this gap.

Reported results are internally inconsistent or insufficiently explained. GPQA uses the same stated accuracy but changes from 3.31 to 1.60 baseline TPS and from 16.36 to 25.00 SlowFast TPS across tables, producing 4.94x versus 15.63x speedups. Table 2 also reports an incorrect relative speedup increment for MBPP. Such discrepancies undermine the headline claims.

SlowFast Sampling is intuitive and training-free, combining confidence-based token selection with adaptive region-level decoding. The exploratory/accelerated-stage presentation makes the high-level idea easy to understand.

The empirical scope is promising: experiments cover eight reasoning, general-knowledge, and coding benchmarks and two diffusion models, LLaDA 8B and Dream 7B. The reported throughput gains are substantial while task scores are often close to the original models.

The paper investigates several central thresholds and stability parameters and demonstrates compatibility with dLLM-Cache. The resulting speed-quality trade-off could be practically useful if validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: The method is not specified precisely enough to reproduce. Important details such as k_slow, k_fast, the duration and termination of the accelerated stage, diffusion-step accounting across cycles, treatment of non-integer e_cycle, and the precise semantics of out-of-span caching are missing. There is also a direct inconsistency: Equation 9 defines e_cycle as the mean of the final history window, whereas the following paragraph says it is the last candidate horizon.

The three claimed “golden principles” receive little rigorous support. A single qualitative visualization does not establish that confidence predicts correctness, that convergence reliably predicts token stability, or that high-confidence tokens form exploitable contiguous regions across tasks and models. Quantitative diagnostics and component-wise ablations are needed to connect these observations to the gains.

The baseline evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier efficiency paper. Comparisons primarily use vanilla diffusion, semi-autoregressive decoding, and an autoregressive model; there is no comprehensive comparison against recent adaptive or accelerated dLLM decoding methods. There is also no cache-only baseline, so the claimed benefit and compatibility of combining SlowFast with dLLM-Cache cannot be isolated.

The efficiency protocol is substantially under-documented: batch size, precision, compilation or kernel settings, prompt and generation lengths for most tables, number of diffusion evaluations, warm-up and timing procedures, and run-to-run variation are absent. TPS values for apparently related GSM8K and GPQA settings differ considerably across Tables 1, 3, and 4 without sufficient explanation, making the headline speedups difficult to audit.

Accuracy differences are reported without uncertainty or significance analysis, despite several benchmarks being small and some purported improvements being unexpectedly large—for example, +4.45 MMLU accuracy from approximate decoding. It is therefore unclear whether the method genuinely preserves or improves quality or whether differences arise from decoding stochasticity or evaluation configuration.

Reproducibility is weak: the “Code:” field is empty, no pseudocode or complete configuration is provided, and several implementation decisions remain ambiguous. The presentation also contains numerous grammatical errors, typographical issues, inconsistent table references, and overstrong claims such as surpassing autoregressive models in practicality based largely on one GPQA throughput comparison.

Overall, the idea and reported results are encouraging, but the missing algorithmic details, limited principle validation, inadequate baselines, and incomplete measurement protocol are major rather than marginal weaknesses. They prevent confident verification of the central efficiency claims at a top-tier conference standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing diffusion-language-model inference latency through a training-free adaptive sampling strategy.
SlowFast is intuitive and potentially useful, combining confidence-based token selection, convergence detection, and regional decoding in a cache-compatible framework.

The empirical study covers two diffusion LLMs and eight benchmarks, reports both throughput and task quality, and includes comparisons with Fast-dLLM, cache-augmented decoding, and limited hyperparameter sensitivity analyses.
Several reported speedups are substantial while preserving accuracy reasonably well, especially for SlowFast without caching.
weaknesses: The central 'golden principles' are mostly intuitive or already implicit in confidence-based remasking. Convergence and positional clustering are supported primarily by selected visual examples rather than aggregate statistics, and there are no component ablations establishing which principle causes the gains.

The method is insufficiently and inconsistently specified. Values for k_slow and k_fast are not reported; caching semantics are unclear; the prose alternately defines the span endpoint as the mean or last candidate; and behavior for an empty candidate set or a non-integer mean endpoint is undefined.

Algorithm 1 appears technically incorrect as written: after decoding only a subset of high-confidence tokens in a span, it advances s_cycle to e_cycle, potentially abandoning still-masked earlier positions. It can also fail to make forward progress when the endpoint equals the current start, yet returns y^(0) without proving that all positions are decoded.

The systems evaluation lacks essential controls: precision, batch size, software stack, compilation settings, timing protocol, warm-up, number of repetitions, variance, memory usage, and hardware utilization are omitted. Consequently, TPS comparisons—especially against LLaMA3—are not demonstrably apples-to-apples.

Important results are internally unclear or inconsistent. GPQA uses both 5-shot/256-token and 8-shot/1024-token settings; Table 3 does not identify its task and reports a SlowFast TPS inconsistent with the apparent GSM8K result; and the headline 34.22x configuration reduces accuracy from 31.47 to 28.79, undermining the characterization of a minor or comparable drop.

Baseline coverage is incomplete for a systems paper. Semi-autoregressive decoding is evaluated only in an ambiguously labeled small table, and cited acceleration methods such as dKV-Cache and Sparse-dLLM are not compared. There are also no controlled ablations isolating endpoint detection, regional decoding, confidence thresholding, and caching.
No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics are reported, which is particularly problematic for small benchmarks such as GPQA. Some claimed accuracy improvements may be evaluation noise.

Although the paper claims reproducibility through supplementary code, the manuscript omits crucial implementation and measurement details. The combination of algorithmic ambiguities, inconsistent reporting, and insufficiently controlled timing evidence prevents verification of the central claims.

strengths: The problem is timely and practically important: reducing the high iterative-decoding cost of diffusion language models could materially improve their usefulness.
The slow/fast decoding intuition is easy to understand, and the paper presents the method with helpful visualizations, pseudocode, and sensitivity analyses.

Experiments cover two diffusion LLMs and eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, knowledge, and code generation. Many reported results show substantial throughput gains with relatively small quality changes.
The method appears compatible with an existing cache-based accelerator, suggesting that sampling and systems optimizations may be complementary.
weaknesses: The three “golden principles” are presented largely as qualitative observations rather than rigorously established findings. The evidence consists mainly of selected confidence plots and case studies; there is no dataset-level analysis measuring confidence calibration, token persistence, convergence, or spatial clustering. Consequently, the central mechanism is not convincingly validated.

The method is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Important quantities such as k_slow and k_fast are not defined or reported in the experimental configuration. The text alternately sets the convergence endpoint to the mean and to the last candidate, and does not precisely define when the accelerated stage terminates. The pseudocode also has questionable state/step updates when stability is detected and may fail to ensure progress when endpoints repeat.

The endpoint criterion is weakly justified: it selects the furthest position whose confidence exceeds a low threshold, even if intervening positions are unstable. Stability of this endpoint over a two-step window does not establish convergence of the tokens inside the span. No ablation directly isolates the endpoint, variance, positional, and confidence components against matched simpler heuristics.

Several reported settings and results are difficult to reconcile. GPQA uses 5-shot/256-token settings in the appendix but 8-shot/1024-token settings for the headline result; Table 3 reports 9.87 TPS for SlowFast on GSM8K while Table 1 reports 14.57 TPS with the same 69.59 score; and some speed-difference annotations appear arithmetically inconsistent. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the evaluation.

The timing methodology lacks essential details such as batch size, numerical precision, prompt and generated-token accounting, stopping behavior, warm-up, compilation, number of runs, and variance. Reporting single TPS and accuracy values without uncertainty makes it impossible to assess whether small quality gains or losses are meaningful.

The headline 15.63x and 34.22x results come from a special long-generation GPQA configuration and comparison against an unusually slow vanilla diffusion baseline. The largest cached speedup also lowers accuracy from 31.47 to 28.79, so the claim of comparable quality is overstated.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. Although the related-work section discusses dKV-Cache, Sparse-dLLM, and exact/advanced diffusion samplers, the experiments primarily compare against Fast-dLLM and basic sampling variants. There is no controlled quality-matched or latency-matched comparison against the broader set of contemporary accelerators.

The comparison with LLaMA3 8B does not establish superiority over autoregressive inference: it compares different model architectures and quality levels without controlling kernels, precision, batching, output lengths, or serving setup. Throughput alone is insufficient for the paper's broad conclusion that dLLMs can outperform autoregressive LLMs in practicality.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the reproducibility statement. Hardware is only described as RTX 4090 GPUs, important algorithmic and timing details are absent, and the experimental tables contain ambiguities. Overall, the promising empirical direction is not supported with the technical precision and controlled evaluation expected at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck for diffusion language models and proposes an intuitive dynamic decoding strategy based on confidence, convergence, and positional locality.
The evaluation covers two representative diffusion LLMs and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, general knowledge, reasoning, and code generation.
The reported speed improvements are substantial: SlowFast generally improves throughput over vanilla decoding and Fast-dLLM while retaining competitive task performance.
Compatibility with dLLM-Cache is practically valuable, and the paper includes sensitivity analyses across several hyperparameters, tasks, and both model families.
The presentation is visually clear, and the case studies make the intended slow/fast behavior easy to understand.
weaknesses: The stated algorithm has a potentially serious correctness problem: after one fast-stage update, it advances the start position to the end of the span even though only tokens above the confidence threshold—or a top-k fallback—are unmasked. Any remaining masked positions in that span appear never to be revisited. This discrepancy between the algorithm, prose, and presumably the implementation undermines technical soundness.

Important details needed to define and reproduce the method are missing or contradictory. In particular, k_slow and k_fast are not reported; the prose alternately defines the span endpoint as the mean and the last candidate horizon; rounding of the mean endpoint is unspecified; and the precise caching operation is insufficiently formalized.

The three proposed principles are supported mainly by selected visual examples rather than quantitative corpus-level evidence. There is no measurement of confidence calibration, token-stability prediction accuracy, prevalence of contiguous stable regions, or causal ablation isolating each principle.

The speed evaluation is not sufficiently controlled for the strongest claims. TPS is reported without end-to-end latency, batch size, precision, compilation settings, memory usage, warm-up protocol, or uncertainty across repeated runs. Comparing fixed-length diffusion generation with an autoregressive model using TPS can also be misleading unless generated-token accounting and stopping behavior are matched.

Several presentation and evaluation inconsistencies reduce confidence: Table 3 reports substantially different SlowFast throughput from Table 1 for apparently the same GSM8K setting; GPQA uses different prompt and generation configurations across tables; and some reported accuracy changes are large despite no confidence intervals or repeated-seed analysis.

Claims of lossless or comparable quality are overstated. Cache-augmented Dream loses roughly 3–5 accuracy points on several tasks, and the 34.22x headline result lowers GPQA accuracy from 31.47 to 28.79.

The baseline coverage is narrow for a top-tier systems/efficient-inference contribution, and there is no matched quality-throughput frontier against broader adaptive-step, speculative, or contemporary diffusion-sampling approaches.

Although the empirical scope and practical motivation are positive, the unresolved algorithmic ambiguity, incomplete reproducibility information, and insufficiently rigorous efficiency comparison prevent the work from meeting the technical-evidence standard for acceptance.
